$comment: Conformance corpus. Every harness's redaction engine runs THIS file, so the
three implementations cannot drift in behaviour even though each is written
in its own language against its own tool pipeline.
`redact` entries must be masked and must name the rule that caught them.
`allow` entries must pass through untouched, and each carries the reason —
the allow half is the half that keeps the guard usable, because a redactor
that mangles placeholders and prose gets switched off, and then it protects
Every credential-shaped literal here is SYNTHETIC: a real prefix followed by
a repeated filler character. They are shaped like secrets on purpose (that
is the point of the test) and are not secrets.

The AWS documentation key is in `redact`, not `allow`: Gitleaks allowlists `.+EXAMPLE$` because it scans repositories, where flagging documentation is noise. Redacting a transcript trades the other way — over-masking a doc key costs nothing, under-masking costs a leak.

redact.input:
-----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----
WWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWW
-----END OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----

-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX
-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
machine api.example.com login bot password zzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzz

allow.why: an env-var reference, not a value — masking it would hide a MISSING credential

documented boundary: the name rule matches api_key/access_key/private_key, NOT a bare _KEY — matching bare 'key' would fire on PUBLIC_KEY, KEY_NAME, keyboard, and a guard that cries wolf gets switched off
an ssh remote, not basic auth

allow.input: The machine learning password policy doc

allow.why: too short to be a github token
a bare prefix with no body
